# Small Binomial Distribution

## 1. Population Description

The fourth distribution is a small binomial distribution with (5) trials and success probability (p=0.10). Each observation counts the number of successes in five trials.

The theoretical mean is:

$$\mu=np=5(0.10)=0.5$$

The theoretical standard deviation is:

$$\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{5(0.10)(0.90)}\approx 0.6708$$

This is a discrete, bounded, right-skewed distribution. It is not heavy-tailed. The observations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed. In R, it can be generated with `rbinom()`.

## 2. Prediction Before the Simulation

Before running the simulation, I predict that the sampling distribution will be right-skewed for small sample sizes because the original binomial population is right-skewed.

As the sample size increases, I expect the sampling distribution to become more symmetric and approximately normal. I also expect the sample means to be centered near the theoretical mean of (0.5), while the standard error decreases.

## 3. Simulation Design

### Sample Sizes

I will investigate the sample sizes (n=5), (n=10), (n=20), (n=30), (n=50), and (n=100).

These sample sizes allow me to observe how the sampling distribution changes as the sample size increases.

### Number of Simulations

For each sample size, I will generate 10,000 repeated samples. Each repeated sample will produce one sample mean.

The sample size (n) is the number of binomial observations in one sample. The number of simulations (B) is the number of repeated samples generated for each value of (n).

```{r}
sample_sizes <- c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100)

B <- 10000
```

### Reproducibility

I used the last four digits of my student ID as the random seed.

```{r}
student_id <- 6424

set.seed(student_id)
```

## 4. Simulation Function

The following function repeatedly samples from the small binomial population and calculates the mean of each sample.

```{r}
simulate_binomial_means <- function(n, B = 10000) {
  replicate(
    B,
    mean(
      rbinom(
        n,
        size = 5,
        prob = 0.10
      )
    )
  )
}
```

I first tested the function using (n=5).

```{r}
test_sample_means_n5 <- simulate_binomial_means(
  n = 5,
  B = B
)

head(test_sample_means_n5)

length(test_sample_means_n5)
```

## 5. Simulation Results

### 5.1 Generating Sample Means for Each Sample Size

```{r}
all_sample_means <- lapply(
  sample_sizes,
  function(n) {
    simulate_binomial_means(
      n = n,
      B = B
    )
  }
)

names(all_sample_means) <- paste0("n_", sample_sizes)

sample_means_n5 <- all_sample_means[["n_5"]]

sample_means_n30 <- all_sample_means[["n_30"]]

sapply(all_sample_means, length)
```

Each sample size should produce 10,000 sample means.

### 5.2 Comparison of Histograms Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
binomial_mean <- 0.5

binomial_sd <- sqrt(5 * 0.10 * 0.90)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

for (n in sample_sizes) {
  
  x <- all_sample_means[[paste0("n_", n)]]
  
  hist(
    x,
    breaks = 30,
    probability = TRUE,
    main = paste("Sampling Distribution, n =", n),
    xlab = "Sample means",
    col = "lightblue",
    border = "white"
  )
  
  curve(
    dnorm(
      x,
      mean = binomial_mean,
      sd = binomial_sd / sqrt(n)
    ),
    add = TRUE,
    col = "darkblue",
    lwd = 2
  )
  
  abline(
    v = binomial_mean,
    col = "red",
    lwd = 2
  )
}

par(old_par)
```

The blue curve represents the theoretical normal approximation. The red line marks the theoretical mean of (0.5).

### 5.3 Normal Q–Q Plots

```{r}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

qqnorm(
  sample_means_n5,
  main = "Normal Q-Q Plot for n = 5"
)

qqline(
  sample_means_n5,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

qqnorm(
  sample_means_n30,
  main = "Normal Q-Q Plot for n = 30"
)

qqline(
  sample_means_n30,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

par(old_par)
```

Points that follow the reference line provide evidence that the sampling distribution is approximately normal.

### 5.4 Numerical Summary Across All Sample Sizes

```{r}
summary_table <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    sample_sizes,
    function(n) {
      
      x <- all_sample_means[[paste0("n_", n)]]
      
      data.frame(
        sample_size = n,
        theoretical_mean = binomial_mean,
        simulated_mean = mean(x),
        simulated_standard_error = sd(x),
        theoretical_standard_error = binomial_sd / sqrt(n),
        skewness = mean(
          (x - mean(x))^3
        ) / sd(x)^3,
        excess_kurtosis = mean(
          (x - mean(x))^4
        ) / sd(x)^4 - 3
      )
    }
  )
)

summary_table
```

This table compares the theoretical and simulated means, standard errors, skewness, and excess kurtosis.

## 6. When Did the Sampling Distribution Become Approximately Normal?

The sampling distribution became approximately normal at (n=30).

At (n=5), the distribution was discrete and showed noticeable irregularity. By (n=30), the histogram was roughly bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot was mostly linear. The simulated mean was (0.5010), close to the theoretical mean of (0.5). The simulated standard error was (0.1217), close to the theoretical value of (0.1225).

Therefore:

$$\boxed{n=30}$$

## 7. Why Did I Choose That Value?

I chose (n=30) because it was the first sample size that produced a reasonably bell-shaped histogram and a mostly linear Q–Q plot. The skewness also decreased from (0.533) at (n=5) to (0.207) at (n=30).

## 8. What Surprised Me?

I was surprised that the sampling distribution was still somewhat irregular at (n=5), even though the sample means were centered near (0.5). The distribution became much smoother and more normal as the sample size increased.

## 9. Conclusion

For the small binomial population, the sampling distribution became approximately normal at (n=30). The sample means stayed near (0.5), the standard error decreased, and the skewness became smaller as the sample size increased. This demonstrates the Central Limit Theorem for a discrete, right-skewed population.
